subtitle: "Wire up smart plugs, sensors, and cameras that react to the real world — no robotics degree needed"

> **In short:** "Physical AI" just means everyday devices using sensors and on-device AI to react to what's happening around them — lights that turn on when you enter, cameras that recognize packages, plugs that switch off when no one's there. You can wire up working automations with off-the-shelf products in an afternoon, without writing code.

The lights turn on when you walk in. A camera tells you a delivery just landed. None of this needs a robotics degree — just a hub app on your phone, a smart plug or two, and one motion sensor.

## Before you start

You'll need:

- A smartphone (iOS or Android)
- 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi where your devices will live (most cheap plugs and sensors won't join a 5 GHz-only network)
- **One starter device** — a TP-Link Kasa smart plug (around $10) or a Philips Hue starter kit (around $30) is the cheapest way in
- A free account in one hub app: **Google Home**, **Samsung SmartThings**, or **Apple Home** (iOS only)
- Optional, for later steps: an **Aqara** or **SwitchBot** motion sensor (around $20), a **Google Nest** or **Arlo** camera (subscriptions from about $3/month are required for person and package detection), and an Alexa- or Google Assistant-enabled speaker

Most smart devices need their **own brand app first** to pair, and **then** get linked into your hub app. We'll walk through both halves.

## Step 1 — Choose your hub app

Open your phone's app store and install **one** hub: Samsung SmartThings, Google Home, or Apple Home. All three can talk to most major-brand smart plugs, lights, and sensors you'll buy.

💬 If you already use Android, **Google Home** is the lowest-friction pick. iPhone family? **Apple Home** keeps more processing local (faster, more private). **SmartThings** supports the widest range of brands.

You'll know it worked when you can sign in and see an empty dashboard with an "Add device" or "+" button waiting.

## Step 2 — Pair a smart plug to its brand app first

Plug your Kasa (or similar) smart plug into a wall outlet. Open its own app — *Kasa Smart* — and tap the **"+"** button to add a device. The app walks you through connecting the plug to your 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and asks you to name it after what it controls.

💬 Suggested device name: `Lamp` or `Coffee machine` — clearer names make later automations easier to find in dropdown menus.

You'll know it worked when tapping the on/off toggle inside the Kasa app produces a quiet relay click from the plug.

## Step 3 — Link the device into your hub

In your hub app (SmartThings or Google Home), look for an option to **"Add device"** or to **link a partner service**. Google Home calls this **"Works with Google"**; in SmartThings, look under each device's settings or in the main settings area for something like **"Linked services"** or **"Partner integrations"**. Pick the brand you just set up — Kasa, Hue, or whichever — and sign in with the same account you used in Step 2.

💬 To check whether a device you already own will work, search its brand name plus "Works with Google" or "SmartThings compatible" before buying anything new.

You'll know it worked when the same plug now appears in **both** the brand app and your hub app, and you can toggle it from either place.

## Step 4 — Build a motion-triggered automation

Add a motion sensor the same way you added the plug — brand app first (Aqara Home, SwitchBot, or whatever your sensor uses), then link that account into your hub. Now create a rule.

In SmartThings: open **Automations** and tap **Add routine**, then choose **If [motion sensor] detects motion → Then [turn on the lamp plug]**.
In Google Home: open **Automations → Create**, set **Starter: motion detected → Action: turn on plug**.

💬 Rule to copy: `If "Hallway Motion" detects motion → Then turn on "Lamp". Only between sunset and sunrise.` Time restrictions stop daytime false triggers.

You'll know it worked when you walk past the sensor at night and the lamp turns on within roughly a second, and stays on until you add an "off after X minutes" finish action.

## Step 5 — Turn on person or package detection on a camera

If you have a **Google Nest** or **Arlo** camera, open its own app and look in **Settings** for options called **Activity zones**, **Familiar faces**, or **Smart alerts**. There you'll find toggles for person-only alerts, package detection, or vehicle detection (availability depends on your model and subscription tier).

💬 Setting name to enable: **"Familiar face detection"** on Nest, or **"Package detection"** on Arlo. Both need their respective subscription plans active.

You'll know it worked when the next push notification says **"Person detected: Anna"** instead of a generic "Motion detected," and only fires for the kinds of events you care about.

## Step 6 — Add a voice routine

Open the **Google Home** or **Alexa** app and find **Routines** — in Alexa, tap **More → Routines**; in Google Home, tap **Settings → Routines** then **Add a routine**. Choose a voice phrase as the trigger and one or more device actions as the result.

💬 Phrase to copy: *"Alexa, start my morning"* — Action: turn on the kitchen plug, read my calendar, and play the news. You can also set a schedule so it runs automatically at 7 a.m. on weekdays.

You'll know it worked when saying the phrase out loud makes the lamp, plug, or speaker react within a second or two, even from another room.

## Common mistakes

- **Buying only 5 GHz-capable devices.** Most cheap smart plugs, bulbs, and sensors only speak 2.4 GHz. Fix: if your router merges both bands under one name, split them in your router settings first, or the device simply won't pair.
- **Skipping the brand app.** Many devices **must** be claimed in their own app first (Kasa, Hue, Arlo, Aqara). Fix: always complete the brand-app pairing in Step 2 before trying to add the device to SmartThings or Google Home, or it fails silently and the device never shows up.
- **Stacking too many rules on day one.** One reliable automation teaches you more than five flaky ones. Fix: build one rule, test it by walking past the sensor five times in a row, then add the next.
- **Ignoring firmware updates.** A camera that didn't recognize packages last year may after a software update — the AI on these devices genuinely improves over time. Fix: let the device app run its update prompt before adding more automations.

## What this means for you

- **At home:** One smart plug plus one motion sensor is a working "physical AI" setup for under $40. Lights respond to you, and the house looks occupied even when it isn't.
- **At work:** A smart plug with a motion sensor cuts phantom power in meeting rooms; a temperature sensor with a fan plug can protect a server closet without a full HVAC overhaul.
- **If you're a beginner:** Pick the hub app you already use (Google or Apple), buy one compatible plug, and complete Steps 2 and 3 today. The rest is repetition, not rocket science.
